title: Leafminer
summary: Leafminer, also reported under the name Raspite, is a regional espionage activity set documented since at least 2017 with victims in government, financial, energy, aviation and telecommunications organisations across the Middle East. Public reporting describes a preference for obtaining access rather than forcing it: watering hole compromise of legitimate local websites that the target audience already trusts, credential harvesting pages that imitate familiar services, and opportunistic exploitation of unpatched public facing systems. The tooling mix has been described as largely publicly available, with custom components used mainly to sustain access, and the operators have been reported to re-register or reuse infrastructure across campaigns. Because much of the activity rides on valid credentials and ordinary web traffic, signature based detection adds little. Useful evidence lives in web proxy logs showing requests to newly registered or lookalike domains, authentication records showing successful logins from unexpected networks, mailbox and file access patterns that exceed a user's normal role, and web server logs showing modification of hosted content. Investigators should also check for web shells and unauthorised accounts on internet facing systems, since these are commonly how the foothold persists. Two misunderstandings recur. The first is that a watering hole must involve a browser exploit, when in practice credential theft is often sufficient. The second is that regional targeting means low sophistication; the observed tradecraft is deliberate, and the local language and cultural knowledge used in the lures is itself an operational capability.

beginner.definition: Leafminer is a name used for a spying group in the Middle East. Public reports describe its activity since around 2017. The reports link it to Iranian state interests, but that link is an assessment rather than a proven fact. The group is known for changing trusted websites and for building fake sign-in pages. Its main goal is to steal working usernames and passwords.
beginner.whyItMatters: A stolen password does not look like an attack. The intruder signs in as a normal employee, so no harmful file appears on any computer. Most companies notice a break-in only when something is deleted or encrypted. Quiet access can last for months. Protecting accounts, not only devices, is what limits the damage.
howItWorks: The attacker finds websites that employees of the target organisation visit often.
A flaw in that website allows the attacker to add hidden content to its pages.
Visitors are sent to a fake sign-in page that copies the look of a real service.
The username and password typed on that page are recorded by the attacker.
The attacker signs in, reads mail and files, and collects more credentials.
Web shells and extra accounts are left behind to keep access after a clean-up.
beginner.example: Picture the keypad at the entrance of an office. A visitor sticks a thin sheet over the keypad that copies every code typed into it. The sheet is transparent, so the keypad still works and the door still opens. Nobody reports a fault, because nothing is broken. The intruder simply collects the codes later and walks in through the front door like an employee. Stealing a password works the same way: the lock is untouched, and the entrance is used exactly as designed.
takeaways: Carefully check the web address before you type a password on any sign-in page.
Use multi factor authentication so a stolen password alone cannot open an account.
Review new accounts and uploaded files on internet facing servers on a regular schedule.

objectives: Explain how a watering hole attack works and why credential theft often needs no exploit.
Identify lookalike domains and newly registered domains in web proxy logs.
Describe how multi factor authentication limits the value of a stolen password.
Explain how web shells and extra accounts are used to keep access to a server.
State the limits of public attribution for this group and why region matters.
